Brandenburg kept close to the Ohio River: schools, storefronts, civic halls, quiet neighbourhoods, and the paddlewheel turning at the landing. Keeping a river town standing meant knowing how to build, mend, and make do.
Dixie was a roadside settlement of diners, pumps, trailers, and stores serving whoever came down the highway. Making something worthwhile from simple supplies became second nature.

Echo Creek gathered around fields, trailers, roadside pumps, church steps, and the water winding through the trees. Hunting country and long drives made careful hands around a firearm part of everyday life.
Ekron lived by its railway, college halls, workshops, and factory floor. Practical work mattered here, and hot metal in capable hands could solve most problems.
Fallas Lake offered still water, open country, hunting trips, and a general store stocked for rural life. Out here, a steady hand was more useful than hurried thinking.

Irvington balanced quiet streets and working farms with cattle yards, rural stores, workshops, and the roar of its famous speedway. Knowing how to coax a living from Kentucky soil was simply part of life here.

Louisville rose above the Ohio River in towers, crowded neighbourhoods, shopping districts, civic halls, and streets that never truly stood still. City life taught you to keep moving and find a path through the crowd.
Muldraugh grew along one hard-working highway: garages, warehouses, diners, motels, and traffic passing through. You learned to keep machines running and yourself moving.

Home could have been anywhere in Knox Country. Every town has the same porches, the same diners, the same slow Sunday mornings. Maybe it never mattered which one was yours - let the county pick this time.
A fresh start, wherever the county sends you
Life followed the Ohio River here: quiet streets, busy shops, the country club, and long afternoons by the water. Riverside always felt settled and familiar.
Rosewood promised tidy streets, front porches, Friday nights at the drive-in, and neighbours who knew your name. Its routines taught you how to hold onto better days.
West Point packed busy streets and old neighbourhoods against the Ohio River. Beyond the last houses, familiar woodland offered food, cover, and a way around town.
